Provide a complete clinical overview and management guide for Pulmonary Nodule.

**Condition:** Pulmonary Nodule
**Category:** Pulmonary Nodule
**Definition:** A spot on the lung, smaller than 3 centimeters (or less than 30 millimeters), that looks different from surrounding normal lung tissue on imaging tests.

**Symptoms:** Small lung nodules rarely cause symptoms; Chest pain; Shortness of breath (dyspnea) or wheezing; Chronic cough or coughing up blood; Fatigue; Hoarseness; Loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss; Recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia

**Causes:** Infections; Inhaled particles; Inflammatory conditions; Scarring (fibrosis); Cancer

**Diagnosis:** Chest X-rays; CT scan (including active surveillance every 6 to 12 months); PET scan; Blood tests (to look for infections or other causes); Sputum tests (to look for infections or other causes); Tissue sample (biopsy) including Bronchoscopy, Thoracoscopy, Video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS), and Needle biopsy; Removing the entire nodule

**Treatments:** Small, noncancerous lung nodules usually don't require treatment; Active surveillance with additional imaging in 6 to 12 months; Medications for infection-caused nodules (antibiotics or antifungal medications); Surgery (if the nodule grows, causes symptoms, or blocks an airway)

**Complications:** Small possibility of being cancerous; Pressing against or blocking an airway (rare for noncancerous nodules)

**Outlook:** Most lung nodules are benign (not cancerous); Benign nodules will usually stay the same size or go away on their own; Nodules staying the same size during a two-year surveillance period are unlikely to be cancer; Nodules smaller than 0.6 cm and those with smooth edges are less likely to be cancerous; Nodules <5 mm have a <1% chance of being cancerous; Nodules 5 mm to 10 mm have up to a 28% chance of being cancerous; Nodules >2 cm (approaching lung mass size) have a 64% to 82% chance of malignancy; Nodules can sometimes begin to grow

**Living With & Management:** Follow up with healthcare provider for additional tests or surveillance; Monitor for symptoms like shortness of breath or chronic cough; Seek ER/911 for chest pain, difficulty breathing, or coughing up blood

Provide a complete clinical overview and management guide for Lung Mass.

**Condition:** Lung Mass
**Category:** Lung Mass
**Definition:** An abnormal area in the lungs larger than 3 centimeters (about 1.5 inches). More likely to be malignant compared to a lung nodule.

**Symptoms:** Chronic cough; Chest pain; Blood-tinged sputum / coughing up blood; Shortness of breath; Lung pain; Shoulder pain; Back pain; Unexplained weight loss

**Causes:** Primary lung cancer; Metastatic cancer from other body parts (breast, colon, bladder cancer); Benign lung tumors; Lung abscesses; AV malformations; Lipoid pneumonia; Pulmonary artery aneurysms; Amyloidosis; Fungal infections; Parasitic infections

**Diagnosis:** Medical history and physical examination; Chest X-ray; CT scan; MRI scan; PET scan (detects increased metabolic activity); Bronchoscopy (with or without Endobronchial ultrasound for central mass near large airways); Fine needle biopsy (for mass in outer lung regions); Thoracic surgery / Lung surgery (Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery [VATS] or traditional thoracotomy)

**Treatments:** Surgery; Chemotherapy; Radiation therapy; Immunotherapy; Treatments specific to non-cancerous causes (e.g., for infections based on specific diagnosis)

**Complications:** Some benign causes can cause serious health complications; Malignancy / cancer spread

**Outlook:** Most often diagnosed as lung cancer (especially with a history of smoking); More concerning if described as 'ground glass' on imaging; Typically benign if stable for two years; Benign tumors are more likely if showing calcifications, fat, or cavitary shapes
